items.text: A game's projected total no longer appears to contradict itself. On the EV Tracker a game showed a projected total of 8.5 while its own detail page showed 7.4, which reads like one of them is wrong. Neither was. Those are two different models: the headline projection is our champion total-runs model, the one the over/under pick is priced against, while the “Predictive distribution” panel is built by a separate per-side run model that estimates each team's runs and adds them together. They usually land about a run apart, so the gap you saw was the normal disagreement between them — it only looked like a defect because both numbers were labelled “Proj.” The panel's figure is now called “Distribution mean” and says outright that it comes from a different model, so an unequal pair reads as two honest estimates rather than a bug. Neither number is a bet recommendation.

When you agree to our terms, we now make sure that agreement is actually recorded. It's worth explaining this one plainly, because nothing looked broken. Accepting the terms wrote a line to our records, and if that write failed — a momentary database hiccup, say — both halves of the system shrugged it off: the server reported success anyway, and the site never checked. That was a reasonable trade when every account was one we'd created by hand, and it stopped being reasonable the moment anyone could sign themselves up, because that record is the only evidence of what you agreed to and when. Three changes: a failed write is now an error rather than a silent shrug, the site retries, and if there's still no record on file you'll be asked to accept the terms the next time you open the site — with links to read them first — and you won't be able to skip past it. That last part also covers a handful of older accounts created before we asked at all. If you've already accepted, you'll never see any of this.

You can now create an account yourself. Until today every “get an account” button on the site — in the top bar, on the home page, on the About page, on the sign-in page and on the membership page — opened an email to Charlie asking for access. That was fine when Credence was invite-only, and it stopped being fine the moment the 2026 Rankings and Projections went out to everyone with a Subscribe button on every withheld number: the path from “I'd like to buy this” to buying it ended in an email and a wait. There's now a Sign Up page, and it takes one click with a Google account. Two smaller things went with it. You come back to where you were: if you started from the membership page, you land back on the membership page ready to subscribe, rather than being dropped on the dashboard having lost what you were trying to do — the same is true of any page that asks you to sign in first. And you'll be shown the Terms and Privacy Policy before you continue, not after. Signing up is free; you subscribe when you want to.

A player's page could show an incomplete career while telling you it was still loading. Opening a player from the Track Record put a “Loading player…” box across the top of the page with his history already drawn underneath it — which looked bad, but the real problem was the history itself. Each past season is fetched separately, so the page was drawing whichever seasons had arrived so far: Jalen Hurts showed three of his seven, with nothing to say the rest were still coming. On the one page whose whole point is the full picture, wins and losses both, a quietly shortened record is worse than a slow one — and it would tend to flatter us, since a season we called badly is just as likely to be one of the slow ones. The page now waits until every season is in before drawing anything.

Player names on the Track Record board were SHOUTING. Veterans came through as “JOSH ALLEN” and “CHRISTIAN MCCAFFREY” while rookies like Ashton Jeanty were spelled normally — 388 of the 563 names across the seven published seasons were in full caps, because veteran and rookie names reach that page from two different sources. They're now spelled the way you'd write them. Two details worth knowing, since perfect casing isn't actually recoverable from a name stored in capitals: “DEVONTA FREEMAN” and “DEVONTA SMITH” are the same word in caps but are correctly Devonta and DeVonta, so names with an unusual capital inside them (CeeDee Lamb, DK Metcalf, JuJu Smith-Schuster) are handled by name; and if we miss a new one, it will show up as a slightly-off capital rather than going back to shouting.

The Track Record headline is now written for a person rather than a statistician. It used to open “our within-position ordering correlation vs realized outcomes is 0.517, against ADP's 0.494 (Δρ +0.022)”, which is accurate and close to unreadable unless you already knew what it meant. It now says what we did (ranked every player against the others at his position, before each season), what happened (our order came out at 0.517 and preseason ADP at 0.494), and what those numbers mean at all — that 1.000 would be a perfect ranking and 0.000 a random one — before saying plainly that we finished ahead by a narrow margin. Every number is still read straight from the scorecard rather than written by hand, the caveat that this is a multi-season average is unchanged, and the wording follows the measurement: if a future season leaves us behind, the sentence says so instead of claiming otherwise.

The Subscribe links on the free 2026 Rankings and Projections pages didn't work. Every lock icon and both “Subscribe to unlock” buttons pointed at a page that doesn't exist, so clicking any of them landed on “page not found” instead of on membership. That shipped at the same time as the free pages themselves, which means the entire path from “I'd like to buy this” to actually buying it was broken for as long as those pages have been open. They now go to the membership page. Two related dead ends went with it: the “Request Beta Access” button on the sign-in page also pointed at a missing page, and the membership page assumed you already had an account — it opened with “sign in to start your membership” and nothing else, which is not much use if you've never been here before. It now lists what a membership includes and offers a way to request access, since accounts are still by request while we finish building.

On the free 2026 Rankings page, the “vs ADP” column showed “NaN” on every row, and our rank, tier and positional rank were simply blank. Those are all part of what a subscription unlocks, so a blank cell was the wrong answer twice over: it looked like a fault rather than a locked value, and blank is also how we show something that genuinely has no value — a distinction we take some care over elsewhere. All four now show a lock, like every other withheld number. Same for Confidence and Range basis on the Projections page. The Export CSV button is now hidden on the free view as well, where it would only have produced a file with the withheld columns empty. And the track record headline — our six-season record against preseason ADP, which is the thing most worth reading on that page — was set in the same small grey type as everything around it; it now leads the page properly.

If you imported an ESPN league, your board was ignoring passing, rushing and receiving YARDS. This was a scoring bug on our side, and it was as bad as it sounds: yardage is the bulk of fantasy scoring, so an ESPN-imported board was ranking players almost entirely on touchdowns and receptions. Every ESPN league was affected from the day ESPN import shipped. The cause was that our ESPN reader was filing those three rules — plus fumbles lost — under slightly the wrong internal names, so they were saved with your league correctly but never reached the scoring step. Nothing was lost or mis-entered on your side, and you don't need to re-import: the fix applies to leagues already saved. The coverage panel on your league page had in fact been reporting these as "saved, not applied" the whole time, which is exactly what that panel is for — we simply hadn't read it. Sleeper and Yahoo imports were never affected. We've added a check that compares every platform's rules against our own list of scoring terms, so a rule can no longer be quietly filed under a name that doesn't exist.

Your league's DEFENSE YARDS-ALLOWED tiers now actually count. If your league pays your D/ST for holding a team under 100 yards and penalises it for giving up 550+ (Sleeper and ESPN both offer this ladder, and it's worth as much as +6 to −7 a game), that rule used to be saved with your league and then ignored, because we didn't project yards allowed. We now do, across all nine tiers your league uses — and because we project how many GAMES a defense is expected to land in each tier rather than a single season total, your league's exact point values are applied as written, not approximated. We also started projecting forced fumbles, two-point conversions, and 40+ yard touchdown bonuses for passing, rushing and receiving, all of which were previously saved-but-ignored. Before turning any of these on, we checked each one against a deliberately dumb baseline — "give every player the league average" — on seasons the model had never seen, and only kept the ones that genuinely beat it. Yards allowed is more predictable year-to-year than points allowed, which our board already used, so it cleared comfortably. One honest caveat: the last three seasons have been a weaker stretch for predicting defensive yardage than the fifteen before them, which we'll re-check after this season.

Four other scoring rules stayed marked "saved, not applied" on purpose, and we think the reason is worth stating. Missed extra points, total fumbles, return touchdowns by a skill player, and fumble-recovery touchdowns were all tested the same way as the rules above, and none of them beat the dumb baseline. Missed extra points is the clearest example: we already project extra points attempted and extra points made, so a missed-PAT projection is one subtraction away and would have taken minutes to add. But 44% of kickers miss none all year and kicker accuracy barely carries from season to season, so that projection would have been noise — and a number built on noise still moves your rankings, while now looking like something we modelled. Leaving it honestly marked as unapplied is the better answer. Return touchdowns and fumble-recovery touchdowns are simpler still: we don't project return usage at all, so there was nothing to build a real projection from.

The MLB prospect board now shows a traded prospect's CURRENT organization, and puts him on the right AL/NL sheet. FanGraphs' board — where the board's org column came from — is an editorial publication, and it does not repoint a player's org when he is traded: across the week of the trade deadline, 47 players on it changed level or rank while exactly zero changed organization. That is not just a wrong label. The org drives the AL/NL filter, which is the filter a single-league dynasty draft actually runs on, so a prospect who changed leagues was either shown as draftable when he was no longer eligible, or missing entirely from the sheet he belonged on. On the current board that was 43 prospects with a stale org and 25 on the wrong league sheet — including River Ryan, the 18th-ranked prospect on the board, who had moved from the Dodgers to the Tigers and so was absent from the AL sheet he should have led. Orgs are now taken from MLB's own data, which tracks two separate signals: which organization's top-30 list a player appears on, and his actual roster assignment. Both of them lag a trade, but in opposite directions and never at the same time — one player sat on his new club's prospect list while his roster still showed the old affiliate, another was still on his old club's list while his roster had already moved — so the board takes whichever of the two has caught up, and treats FanGraphs' org as the older baseline they are compared against. In the rare case where the two disagree with each other about where a player went, the board does NOT guess: it keeps the original org and flags the conflict for review, because moving a player into a league he may not be in is the exact failure this is meant to prevent. A corrected player also loses his FanGraphs organizational rank rather than carrying it across — being "3rd best in the system" refers to the system he left, and asserting it about his new one would be inventing a ranking FanGraphs never published. His prior org and prior org rank are both kept alongside, so you can see what changed and what it used to say.

Past-season fantasy results stay free, and the current season is now locked at the DATA layer rather than only in the interface. If you aren't subscribed, a 2026 projection, rank or range no longer just disappears — the player row is still there, with a lock on each withheld number and a link to subscribe, so you can see exactly what a subscription adds. The important half is invisible: the server never sends a 2026 number it hasn't verified you're entitled to, so those values aren't sitting in the page for anyone who reads the network traffic. Subscribers see no change at all.

The 2026 fantasy Rankings and Projections are now open to everyone, without an account. You'll see every drafted player, his team, bye and market ADP, with our projection, ranking and range shown as locked — each one a link to subscribe rather than a blank cell, so you can see exactly what a subscription adds before paying for it. Past seasons remain fully free, including the track record of how these projections have actually done against preseason ADP over six seasons, which is now linked from the top of both pages. Two things worth being straight about: the free view is ordered by market ADP, not by our ranking — our order is part of what you'd be subscribing for, so it isn't published — and players who went undrafted in the market sample are left off the free page rather than listed with nothing beside them; the count is shown so you know what's missing. Subscribers see no change.

The Settings page now tells you the truth about a canceled subscription. Canceling in the billing portal doesn't cut off access immediately — like most subscriptions, you keep everything you paid for until the current billing period actually ends, and only then does the account step down. But Settings didn't say that: it kept showing "Active subscription" with no hint that anything had changed, so a canceled member had no way to tell whether the cancellation actually went through, short of waiting for access to disappear. It now shows the exact date access continues through and that the plan won't renew after that.

Fixed several info tooltips across the site that couldn't be opened by tapping on a phone. These little “ⓘ” icons — next to stats on the Performance page, team pages, and elsewhere — were built to appear on mouse hover, which doesn't exist on a touchscreen; tapping one did nothing. They now open on tap as well as hover, matching how the fantasy pages' info icons already worked. We also checked every other icon that only reveals information on hover and fixed the ones that had the same problem, and re-verified nothing on the site still needs a mouse to be readable.

There's a new My Teams page under NFL → Fantasy that shows every league you've imported in one place, with each roster scored under that exact league's own scoring format — not a generic PPR guess. Import a league from Sleeper, Yahoo or ESPN, tell us which team is yours (Yahoo does this automatically; Sleeper and ESPN don't hand us that, so you pick it), and your starters and bench show up here with their season projection and 80% range. The number shown is the rest-of-season projection, which before kickoff is effectively the same as the full-season number — we label it that way rather than inventing a fake per-game figure. Any rostered player we couldn't match to a projection is shown honestly rather than silently dropped. Per-game splits, in-season roster updates and waiver-wire suggestions are coming once our weekly model ships — this first version is season-level only.

We swapped the model behind our projected run totals on August 2nd and reverted it the same day. We're leaving this note up rather than deleting it, because the change was briefly live. The idea was that the old model's game-by-game confidence was misleading — that it was most overconfident on the games it called calmest — so we replaced it with one that states a single steady level of uncertainty. Before finalizing, we re-scored both models over the same 1,362 games of this season and checked something the original analysis had not: whether the games it grouped as calm were actually calmer. Grouped that way, the result reversed — the old model was the better-calibrated of the two, including on games it had never been trained on. So the reason for the change didn't hold up, and we put the previous model back. The projected totals and over/under percentages you see are the ones you saw before August 2nd, and the per-game confidence band varies by game again. The honest summary is that neither model's game-by-game uncertainty is as good as we'd like — that's now the thing we're working on, rather than the choice between these two. Nothing here was ever a betting claim: totals bets remain paused, and we make no claim about win rates or returns. The morning (pre-lineup) totals projection was never affected.

Fixed two display bugs on the NFL Rankings board. The highlighted "T#" badge that marks the start of a value tier was re-appearing every time a kicker or defense row broke up a run of ranked skill players — kickers and defenses aren't tiered on purpose (see below), so one real tier could show up as three or four separate same-numbered tiers with a kicker or defense sandwiched in between. The badge now looks past those untiered rows to the last real tier it saw, so it only starts over at an actual value break. Separately, tiers were coming out either far too small or far too large depending on position and format — a lone player at the top of the board as his own tier (Tier 1 showing just the #1 overall player), or, in full-PPR, nearly the entire wide receiver position landing inside just two tiers because a long, gradually-declining stretch of receivers never has one big value break in it. Tiers are still grouped by an unusually large drop-off in value, but every tier is now required to hold a reasonable number of players — scaled to how many players are being tiered, so a shallow position like tight end and a deep one like wide receiver each get a sensible tier count instead of the same fixed number. A tier that would come out too small merges with its neighbor; one that would come out too large (that long receiver stretch) is broken up at its own biggest internal value drops instead of being left as one undifferentiated block.

Bets on late games at the end of a month no longer sit "Pending" forever. A bet settles once we see its game's final score, and we were reading those finals from a schedule feed we pull one calendar month at a time. That works fine all month — but a game that starts after 7pm Pacific on the last day of a month finishes after the calendar has already rolled over, and every pull from then on covered only the new month. So those games never got their final recorded, and any bet on one stayed Pending indefinitely with nothing to flag it: it looked exactly like a game that simply hadn't finished yet. Three bets on July 31st games were stuck this way. They've been settled at their correct results, and two things now prevent a repeat. When our own records don't show a game as final, we now ask MLB directly for the result at settlement time, so a gap in that schedule feed can't strand a bet again — and we only ever accept a result MLB reports as a completed game, never a score from a game still in progress. And any bet still pending more than a day after its game's first pitch now raises an alert to us, because that is a data problem rather than a long game, and until now nothing told the difference.

There's a new Track Record page under NFL Fantasy, and you don't need an account to see it. For every past season back to 2019, it shows what our model would have projected each player, what the market's average draft position said about him, and what he actually did — side by side, no login required. The honest read: on average across those seasons our ordering beats ADP, but not everywhere and not every year — running back is a wash, one season was a loss, and expert ranking sets (FantasyPros, Sleeper) still order players better than we do overall. Where we hold up best is in our highest-conviction disagreements with the market — the picks where we most differ from ADP still come out ahead there. We built it this way on purpose: a track record you can't check isn't a track record, so every number here is a straight recompute of an already-shipped model against seasons that already happened, wins and losses both, and a good chunk of the page is telling you where we don't win. The current season's live projections stay part of the paid product — you'll see a clearly marked, locked card for it on this page and on every player's page — but browsing any past season, and any player's history, is free.

Sleeper league imports now show real player names on your rosters, not raw IDs. Until now, importing a Sleeper league pulled in your teams and draft picks fine, but each rostered player showed only as a number — Sleeper's roster data carries player IDs with no names attached, and resolving them requires a large player file Sleeper's own guidance says apps should fetch at most once a day, so we could not do it live during an import. We now refresh that name file on our own schedule and match it against every roster spot: open the Teams section on the import review page and click a team to see its players by name and position instead of by ID. Draft picks already showed full names and are unchanged. If a player cannot be matched — most often a very recent add before our next refresh — the review page says exactly how many of your rostered players matched and shows the rest by ID rather than hiding them or guessing a name.

The NFL fantasy board now ranks players with our market-aware model. Until now every fantasy surface — Projections, Rankings, the League Board, the Draft Optimizer and the player pages — ordered players purely on our own projection, deliberately ignoring where the market is drafting them. We have been testing a version that also reads consensus draft position, and over six held-out seasons it ordered players better than ADP did overall, where our market-blind board had been ordering slightly worse than ADP. Two things it does NOT change, on purpose: the projected points themselves and the 80% range around them are exactly the same numbers as before — this re-orders the board, it does not re-price anyone — and every player still carries the same per-player range and confidence tier. What it does change is who sits above whom inside a position. Now the honest limits, because they matter more than the headline. The improvement is an average: it is clearly positive at quarterback, wide receiver and tight end, and a wash at running back, and it was negative in one of the six seasons. It is measured against ADP — where the public is drafting — and NOT against expert ranking sets: FantasyPros' consensus and Sleeper's rankings both still order players better than we do, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. And at quarterback, running back and wide receiver the ranking now incorporates the market itself, so it is not an independent read on the market at those positions and we will never present it as one. Each browse surface says which positions use the market, and a player's page says it for his position. Nothing here is betting advice.

You can now import your fantasy league straight from Sleeper, instead of typing its settings in by hand — rolling out to invited accounts first, so it won't appear for everyone yet. Go to Import League under the NFL fantasy pages and enter either your Sleeper username or your league ID — the long number in your league's Sleeper URL — and pick the league you want. We read its scoring and its roster shape — per-yard and touchdown values, PPR including a TE premium, field goals by distance, the full team-defense sheet and the points-allowed tier table, plus every starting slot, FLEX, SUPERFLEX, bench, IR and taxi spot — and save it as one of your leagues. From there it behaves exactly like a league you typed in yourself: the League Board, Rankings and Draft Optimizer all re-score the projections under your rules and recompute value over replacement against your real starting lineup. Sleeper's league data is public, so nothing is asked of you beyond your username — no sign-in, and certainly no Sleeper password. Before anything is saved you get a preview that tells you exactly what we could and could not do with your settings: which of your scoring rules move your board precisely, which ones our projection resolves more coarsely and had to fold together, and which ones we keep on record but genuinely cannot apply because we don't project that stat at all. That last group matters — a rule that quietly scores zero would look identical to one that works, so we name them rather than let you assume. If your league drafts on Sleeper, we also show the picks that have already gone; that part is read fresh every time and never stored, because a stale list of drafted players looks exactly like a correct one.

Yahoo league import is built and waiting on Yahoo. When it switches on you'll sign in on Yahoo's own page, grant read-only access to your leagues, and import them the same way — we never see or hold your Yahoo login, and you can revoke the permission from your Yahoo account settings at any time. Yahoo now reviews every application for access to their fantasy data, so the timing is theirs, not ours; until it clears, the Import League page says so plainly rather than showing you a button that fails.

ESPN league import is here, and it works a little differently on purpose. ESPN publishes no approved way for another app to read a private league — the only automated route would be handling your ESPN sign-in, a credential that isn't read-only, isn't limited to fantasy, and that you couldn't revoke for us specifically. We won't ask you for that. So instead: give us your league ID, we build you a link, you open it in your own browser (where you're already signed in), and you paste back what ESPN shows you. Your browser makes the request; we only ever see the league settings. From there it behaves exactly like Sleeper — we read your scoring, roster shape, teams and rosters, show you the same honest preview of what we could and couldn't apply, and save it as one of your leagues. If you import before your draft there are no rosters yet to bring over; that's expected rather than a failed import, everything the draft tools need is in your settings, and importing again afterwards picks up the rosters. Two things worth knowing, both of which the preview tells you about your specific league rather than leaving you to find out from a scoreboard. ESPN groups team-defense points-allowed slightly differently than we do at one boundary, so a game where your defense allows exactly 21 points scores at your 22-27 rate instead of your 18-21 rate; every other tier matches exactly. And if your league scores its defense on total yards allowed, we save those rules but can't rank on them yet — we don't project yards allowed — so a defense that wins by suppressing yardage will be under-rated on your board. Anything we save without applying is now listed in plain English instead of ESPN's internal rule numbers. If your league is on CBS, MyFantasyLeague or Fantrax, enter it once under My League Settings: it takes a few minutes and every tool then works identically.

The league import preview now says, in one line, that we record which of your league's scoring settings we couldn't apply — the rule and its point value only, never your name, team or roster — so we know which gaps to prioritize closing. This is aggregate bookkeeping on our side, not anything new about what gets saved to your account: your saved league still holds every rule you imported exactly as it did before, applied or not.

You can now enter your league's settings by hand on the NFL fantasy pages, under My League Settings — rolling out to invited accounts first, so it won't appear for everyone yet. Until now you had to pick one of our preset formats — half-PPR, full PPR, superflex and so on — and if your league didn't match one of them, the closest preset was the best you could do. Now you can start from whichever preset is nearest and then change anything: per-yard passing, rushing and receiving values, touchdown values, PPR (including half-point and a TE premium), interceptions, fumbles, two-point conversions, field goals broken out by distance, extra points, and the full team-defense sheet including sacks, takeaways, safeties, blocked kicks and the points-allowed tier table. The roster is fully editable too — any number of FLEX slots, a SUPERFLEX, and bench and IR spots. Save it and the League Board, Rankings and Draft Optimizer all switch to your league: the projections are re-scored under your exact rules, and value over replacement is recomputed against your actual starting lineup, which is what makes a QB and a WR comparable on one board. Bench and IR slots correctly count for nothing there, since they never start. Nothing about this replaces the presets — they're still there and still the default.

The league settings editor tells you which of your settings we actually apply, instead of quietly scoring the rest as zero. Our projections cover offensive skill players, kickers and defenses — but a real league scores things we don't project at all, like a defensive forced fumble or an offensive player recovering a fumble in the end zone. Rather than accept those settings and silently ignore them, the editor labels each one: applied exactly, folded to our resolution, or captured but not applied. Anything in that last group is saved with your league so your settings stay a faithful record, and it plainly says it contributes nothing to the board — we won't invent a number we can't project. The one place we combine rather than apply exactly is field goals: we project them at under-40, 40-49 and 50+, so if your league prices, say, 20-29 and 30-39 differently, those are combined and the editor says so. If your league pays the same for both (nearly all do), it's exact and nothing is lost. Your points-allowed tier table is always applied exactly, including the common 14-20 and 35+ tiers. We've also added a rule you can record that we deliberately don't apply: a second weekly matchup against the league median. It's a real part of many leagues, but it changes win-loss records rather than what any player is projected to score, so it doesn't touch the board — and the editor says that rather than implying otherwise.

Pick email alerts now go out when your lineup-confirmed picks are ready, not in the morning preview. Until now the one pick email you'd get each day fired first thing in the morning, before starting lineups were even announced — so it was showing preliminary picks that could still change once each team's lineup was set a few hours before first pitch. That email is retired. You'll now get an email as soon as new picks become official (H2H moneyline and totals only — player props aren't part of this yet), sent as lineups confirm through the afternoon and evening rather than all at once, and each pick is only ever emailed to you once. Framed the same honest way as always: these are the model's qualified selections, not a promise of profit.

Kickers and defenses (D/ST) are now projected on the NFL fantasy pages. Until now the tools projected offensive skill players only, so the K and D/ST roster slots rendered "not projected" — you could record a pick there, but there was nothing to rank. Both positions now carry a full projection: for kickers, field goals split by distance (under 40, 40-49, 50+) plus extra points; for defenses, sacks, interceptions, fumble recoveries, defensive and special-teams touchdowns, safeties, blocked kicks, and the points-allowed distribution that drives the points-allowed scoring tiers. Because the projection emits those raw components rather than a single points total, your league's own scoring — including distance-based field-goal values and any points-allowed tier table — is applied exactly rather than approximated. They rank, sort, and fill draft slots like every other position.

The kicker and D/ST projections are deliberately modest, and the pages say so. These are the two least predictable fantasy positions and we measured just how much: a kicker's field-goal accuracy carries almost no year-to-year signal (correlation 0.09), and a defense's touchdowns, safeties and blocked kicks are statistically indistinguishable from noise, so those are projected at the league average rather than given a fake team-specific number. What does carry signal is a kicker's team scoring environment (which drives extra-point volume) and his leg strength (the share of his attempts from 50+ yards persists at 0.43), plus a defense's sacks, takeaways and points allowed. So every K and D/ST row carries a wide range, and each page says plainly that these are base projections meant to be read as a streaming tier — better situations versus worse ones — not as a precise rank. The ranges are the honest part: they were checked against 15 seasons of held-out results and cover 83% (kickers) and 90% (defenses) of actual outcomes against an 80% target.

Picks were being flagged "degraded" on days when nothing was actually wrong with the slate. Every pick carries a data-completeness score, and a handful of team-strength inputs (our running team offense, bullpen and win-rate beliefs) had been dropping out for whole days at a time: July 22, 23, 24, 27 and 28 all lost the bullpen belief for every single game. Two separate causes, both now fixed. First, the job that advances those beliefs each night tracked one shared "last day processed" marker for all three of them, so if the bullpen input's source data wasn't ready yet, that day got marked done anyway and the bullpen belief for it was skipped permanently. Each belief now tracks its own progress and retries until its data is ready, so none can be silently skipped. Second, the feature that reads those beliefs required all three to come from the same day's record, so one missing value blanked the others too; each is now looked up independently, falling back to that team's most recent earlier value. The monitor that is supposed to catch this class of problem did not fire, because it averaged over an eight-day window — which needs three of eight days to go fully dark before it notices. It now checks every individual game day, and covers these team-strength inputs, which it previously did not look at at all.

Strikeout prop bets in the Bet Log now close the same night the game ends, instead of sitting on "Pending" for a day or two. Moneyline and totals bets settled within hours of the final out, but a pitcher-strikeout bet was graded off a table built from pitch-tracking data that is only rebuilt once a day — so a prop on a game that had been over since the afternoon could still read Pending the next morning, and sometimes the morning after that. Strikeout props are now graded straight from MLB's official box score as soon as the game is confirmed final, with the pitch-tracking table still used whenever it already has the answer. We checked every strikeout prop ever logged before changing anything: all 16 that had settled were graded CORRECTLY — right side, right result, right profit or loss — so this was a delay, not a wrong answer, and nobody's record was misstated. The one bet that was still open on a finished game has been settled. Bets now also record when they closed, which is what makes a stuck bet visible in future rather than something you have to notice yourself. Two related fixes: a bet that had already been settled could stay in the queue of unsettled bets indefinitely, and it was possible to log an over/under without a line — which meant it could never be graded at all, and one such bet had been showing Pending since July 2nd. Logging a bet without the information needed to settle it is now rejected up front.

Veteran 80% ranges on the NFL fantasy pages are now calibrated against what veterans actually did — and the old ones were badly off. Every range we shipped for the ~700 veterans on the draft board (about 90% of it) was built from a player's game-to-game scoring variability: project his points, then go up and down by a fixed multiple of that. We had checked that method for the ~80 rookies but never once for the veterans. Checking it now against 13 completed seasons and 8,398 veteran seasons: only 55% of veterans finished inside their own 80% range, and it missed in BOTH directions — 27% finished below the bottom of their range and 18% above the top. The reason is that a veteran's biggest risk is not week-to-week scoring noise, it is losing the job or the season: 31% of projected veterans finish a season with exactly zero points. Game-to-game variability measured on the games a player DID play cannot see that coming, and a symmetric range cannot fit a season total that has a hard floor at zero and no ceiling. Ranges are now read off what comparable players actually did — for each player we look at the veterans most similar to him and take their real 10th and 90th percentile outcomes. Coverage goes from 55% to 89%, and every position clears the 80% target on its own: quarterbacks 68% → 86%, running backs 55% → 89%, tight ends 54% → 89%, receivers 51% → 91%. What you will see is HONESTLY WIDER ranges (average width 64 → 101 points), and a bottom-of-range of zero for most mid- and late-round veterans — because for those players, finishing with nothing is genuinely one of the likelier outcomes. Top-tier veterans keep a real floor: Josh Allen's range is 131–447, not 0–447. Projections themselves are completely unchanged — this changes only the uncertainty around them. We also set up an annual re-check of both the rookie and veteran targets, because a range being wrong is invisible until the season is over.

Rookie 80% ranges on the NFL fantasy pages are now held to their target coverage POSITION BY POSITION, not just overall. When we moved rookies to per-player ranges we checked that 80% of rookie seasons landed inside their range across all rookies together — and they did, 81%. Splitting that by position showed the accuracy was not evenly spread: rookie quarterbacks landed inside their range only 74% of the time and running backs 78%, while tight ends were at 87%. An overall number can be met by one position covering for another, and quarterback was the position paying for it — about a third of drafted rookie QBs never take an NFL snap, which makes their outcomes the hardest of any position to bracket. Every position is now required to hit 80% on its own before a range calculation is eligible to ship, and the winning method adds a per-position calibration step on top of the per-player fit. Rookie QB coverage goes from 74% to 81% and running backs from 78% to 80%, with every position now at or above target. The practical effect you will see is that rookie quarterback ranges are slightly WIDER than before — which is the honest direction, not a regression: if a third of rookie QBs score nothing, a range that says so is telling the truth, and a narrower one was simply wrong more often. As before, no rookie's POINT projection changes by even a fraction of a point — this is entirely about the range around it. Two things we would rather state than bury: the position-level check rests on a small number of seasons (about 80 rookie quarterbacks over seven draft classes), so it is met with a thin margin rather than comfortably, and a range is a statement about a distribution of outcomes, never a prediction that any individual player will land inside it.

Player pages were showing an IL badge on players who are healthy and playing. Jesús Luzardo's page read "On IL since 2024-06-19" while he was starting for Philadelphia — and he was not alone: 62 of the 187 players we flagged as currently injured had already played since the date we claimed they went on the IL, some of them stranded there for as long as five seasons. The cause was that a player's injury status only ever cleared when we saw a specific piece of text in MLB's roster feed — "activated from the injured list". If the return was worded any other way ("the Rays activated Drew Rasmussen", full stop), or if the player came back through a roster move instead of a formal activation, or if his reinstatement happened over the winter — when that feed simply is not collected — nothing ever closed the injury out, and the badge stayed on forever. Status is now cleared by any of those returns, and, as a backstop that does not depend on how MLB words anything, by the player appearing in a major-league game: if he has played, he is not on the IL. That last rule is what makes this durable rather than a one-time cleanup. Injury status is also now checked every day against exactly that contradiction — anyone we call injured who has since played — so this cannot go quietly wrong again. A wrong status is worse than no status, and this one was wrong for a long time.

Every rookie on the NFL fantasy Projections page now carries his own 80% range. Until now the rookie range was a class-level bucket: all 81 rookies shared just 12 ranges between them (three per position), so every top-tier rookie QB showed an identical 27–277 while their actual projections spanned 25 to 268 — a 268-point projection sat pinned near the very top of "its own" range and a 25-point rookie at the bottom of the same one. The range is now fitted to each player from his own projection, draft slot and position against what comparable drafted rookies actually went on to score, busts included and counted as zero. Jeremiyah Love, for example, moves from 10–245 to 15–346 around a 208-point projection. Two things worth being clear about: his POINT projection has not changed at all — this is purely about the range around it — and the new rookie ranges are on average slightly WIDER, not narrower, and about twice as wide as a veteran's. That is the honest direction: a rookie has no NFL games to go on, and pretending otherwise would be the easiest way to make these numbers look more confident than they are. The "Class-level" tag disappears for rookies as a result, and the range bar now shows where his projection actually sits inside his own interval.

The NFL fantasy boards were missing players who sat out all of last season. A player with no games in the base season was dropped from the projection universe entirely — the rule exists to keep retired players off the board, but it could not tell a retirement from a season-ending injury, so genuinely draftable names (Brandon Aiyuk, Tank Dell, Jonathon Brooks, MarShawn Lloyd) simply had no row. They are back: a player who missed a full season is now projected off his most recent season actually played, provided he is still on a 2026 roster or depth chart, and retired players are still excluded. Returning players are deliberately discounted rather than projected as if nothing happened — across 431 comparable cases since 2016 a player coming back from a full missed season averaged about 4 games, not the 10 a healthy player does, and 43% never played at all. So each of these rows carries a hard availability haircut, a much wider range, and a Low confidence badge, and it will usually sit below where the draft market ranks him. That gap is intentional, and the ADP column beside it shows you exactly how far apart we are.

A round of refinements to the NFL fantasy boards. Rankings now groups players into tiers — a tier breaks where there is an unusually large drop to the next player, which is the practical draft question: inside a tier you can take whoever you like, but letting a tier run out before your next pick costs you real value. The League Board now names the actual player sitting at each position's replacement level, so 'replacement' stops being an abstract number and becomes 'better than that guy'. Season Projections gains pagination and keeps a player's board position visible when you search for him, instead of renumbering the list. The ADP difference column is now labelled 'vs ADP' rather than a mathematical symbol, and the Confidence column explains itself — it measures how much played history sits behind a projection, which is not the same as how good the player is. Column explanations now open on tap as well as hover, so they work on a phone. Available to subscribers.

Made rookie projection ranges honest about what they are. A rookie has never played an NFL game, so his 80% range is not calculated from his own history — it is a range shared by every rookie drafted around the same slot. Previously that looked identical to a veteran's own range, which made a very wide rookie band read as a precise statement about that player. Rookie ranges are now labelled 'Class-level' and shown muted, with an explanation, so you can tell at a glance which ranges are specific to a player and which are a statement about rookies in general. The underlying projection is unchanged; we are working on genuinely per-player rookie ranges.

Added average draft position (ADP) to the NFL fantasy Rankings and League Board, alongside a difference column showing where our board and the public disagree. ADP is drawn from thousands of real public drafts and is matched to your scoring format and league size — that matching matters: a top quarterback goes around pick 28 in full-PPR but inside the first two picks in superflex, so a single 'ADP' number would be badly misleading on a superflex board. A positive difference means the room typically drafts a player later than we rank him; a negative one means they take him earlier. This is a reference point so you can see where we differ, not a claim that our order is the better one — read it next to the 80% range, which tells you how sure the model actually is. Players nobody is drafting simply show no ADP. Available to subscribers.

Made the NFL fantasy boards easier to read and work with. Column headers for the terms of art — value over replacement, replacement level, next at position, ADP and the ADP difference — now explain themselves on hover, so you no longer have to infer what a column means. Rankings is paginated (50 players a page by default, switchable to 25, 100, or all of them), and you can export the current rankings to CSV — the export includes every player matching your filters, not just the page you are looking at. Available to subscribers.

Opened three NFL fantasy pages under NFL → Fantasy: Projections, Rankings, and the League Board. Projections lists every projectable player's 2026 season line — the passing, rushing and receiving totals we expect, the games we expect them to play, and an 80% range on their fantasy points, so you can see how confident the model is rather than just a single number. Rankings and the League Board take that same projection and re-score it for your league: pick your scoring format (standard, half-PPR, full-PPR, superflex, the 3-WR variants) and your league size, and the board re-ranks accordingly — superflex really does lift quarterbacks, because the roster shape changes how many of them start. The League Board adds value over replacement, which is what makes a quarterback and a running back comparable on one list, and it shows the replacement level it used for each position instead of asking you to take it on faith. Every number is a projection with a range attached, and a wide range is the model telling you it doesn't know — rookies in particular carry very wide ranges because rookie outcomes genuinely are. This is a projection and transparency tool for your own draft decisions; modelling is ongoing, we make no claim that it beats any particular ranking, and nothing here is betting advice. Available to subscribers.

Fixed dropdowns on the fantasy pages opening detached from the control you tapped — on a phone the menu appeared near the top of the screen instead of under the field. The dropdowns are now built the same way as the ones on Bet Log and the Parlay Calculator, which were never affected, so the menu is positioned by the page itself rather than by the browser's built-in picker. The same change covers the search and filter controls on Players and the book pickers in Settings. Separately, number fields no longer fight you when you clear them to retype: clearing a field used to snap it to zero, so the next digit you typed read as "01". On the Kelly cap fields in Settings and the EV Tracker that was worse than cosmetic — clearing the field snapped it to 1, so typing "5" silently left you on 15%, which feeds bet sizing. Those fields now hold exactly what you type and only accept a complete value.

Every player on the NFL fantasy pages now has his own page — click a name on Projections, Rankings, the League Board or the Draft Optimizer to open it, or find anyone directly from the new Player Search page. It brings together his full projected stat line, fantasy points under standard, half-PPR and full-PPR scoring side by side with what he's worth in your own selected league, his 80% range drawn as a band against the realistic spread for his position rather than just printed as two numbers, his position rank, value over replacement and tier, and where the market is drafting him compared to where we have him. Rookie ranges show as real player-specific bands here, the same as everywhere else — only a rookie thin enough on draft history to fall back to the class-level band gets that label, never a per-player one. Nothing new is being calculated; it's the same numbers you'd already see on the boards, gathered onto one page per player.

Four refinements to the new NFL fantasy player page. Fantasy points now show what percentile that projection is within his position — is 260 points a lot for a tight end? Now you can tell at a glance, separately from his league board rank. "Overall Rank" is now labelled as our model's own rank, not a claim about where the market will actually take him — that's what the ADP column next to it is for. A player with no Tier badge now says why instead of just showing a dash — usually that he's below replacement level in your selected format (a QB with no tier in a 1-QB league can very plausibly tier in superflex, so the format matters). And the page now shows a team logo alongside his name.

The NFL fantasy player page now shows a real headshot photo and basic bio info — age, height, weight, college and years in the NFL. The photo is his official NFL.com picture; a small number of players (mostly very recent additions the league's own data hasn't caught up to yet) show his initials instead rather than a broken image.

The NFL fantasy player page now shows what pushes each player's number up or down, player by player — recent scoring pace, age, team offensive environment, and a handful of other signals, each shown in actual points, positive or negative, specific to that player. This comes from a separate research model of ours (not the one behind the projection shown above it), so its own total for a player is not always the exact same number — think of it as a second, independent read on what makes him him, not a receipt for the projection above. Covers QB, RB, WR and TE; kickers and defenses aren't covered by this model. Look for it under a player's draft value on their page.

Subscriber player pages now show a History panel: how that player actually finished in each past season back to 2019, what the market's average draft position said about him that season, and a weekly injury-report log with a games-missed count. This is the same past-season computation already powering the free Track Record page, now attached directly to a player's own page so you don't have to cross-reference the two, plus a genuinely new injury history — every weekly game-report and practice-participation status on file, most recent first. Framed honestly on purpose: the games-missed count is how many of his team's games he didn't play in for any reason (injury, a healthy scratch, a roster move), not a claim that every absence was injury-caused — the weekly report next to it is where a specific injury is actually named, only when one was reported. None of this is a claim about this season; it's a straight recompute of realized history, wins and losses both. A rookie with no past season, or a team defense (a team, not a person), simply has no panel to show.

The player History panel now shows points per game for each past season, alongside the season total, and a plain-language "year-to-year consistency" read — Steady, Somewhat variable, or Boom-or-bust — based on how much that per-game rate has swung across his past seasons. It's built from data the panel already had, so it's showing up for every player who already had a History panel. Deliberately a RATE, not a season total: a year cut short by injury doesn't get punished as inconsistent scoring, since that's a games-missed story, not a performance one — the two are shown separately for exactly that reason. It needs at least three past seasons with games played to say anything, so a player without enough history simply doesn't get a badge rather than a shaky one. This describes what already happened; it isn't a projection of what he'll do this season. A week-to-week (in-season) version of this same idea — how spiky a player is game to game within one season, not season to season — is a separate, tracked follow-on (NF3.6) since it needs a small new data pull, not just this panel's existing numbers.

Added a 'Predictive distribution' section to the totals pick detail page. Instead of just a single projected total, you can now see the model's full calibrated view of how a game's scoring could land: a distribution of the game total with the market line drawn on it and the leaned side shaded, the projected total with an 80% range (the model puts about 80% of the outcomes between those two run values), the probability the total goes over the line, the home-minus-away run-margin view behind the moneyline lean, and P(over) ladders for each team's total and for alternate game-total lines. This is a transparency tool — a calibrated picture of the model's spread and uncertainty, shown so you can see how confident the model is. It is not a bet recommendation: our models have no demonstrated market edge (best alpha = 0), and none of these lines cleared an edge test, so treat everything here as context, not value picks.

Reorganized the top navigation around sports. Instead of one long list, the menu now leads with the sport — MLB today — and groups everything for that sport underneath (your Dashboard, EV Tracker, Props, Parlay Calculator, Performance, Bet Log, and Team/Player research all live under MLB). Nothing moved out of reach: every page is exactly where it was, just gathered under its sport, and all your existing links and bookmarks keep working. This makes room for more sports as they come online — you'll also notice a new NFL section with a Fantasy area, which we're building toward and will open up soon. Your access to everything you use today is unchanged.

Added two-factor authentication (2FA) for extra account security. In Settings → Two-Factor Authentication you can now turn on an authenticator app: scan the QR code (or enter the setup key) in Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, or any similar app, and from then on you'll enter a 6-digit code from that app along with your password each time you sign in. You can turn it back off anytime by re-entering your password. If you sign in with Google, two-factor is already handled by your Google account, so there's nothing extra to set up here.

Added 'Continue with Google' to the sign-in page. You can now sign in with your Google account in one tap instead of typing an email and password — Credence never sees your Google password, and the account you land in works exactly like a regular one. Existing email-and-password sign-in continues to work unchanged.

Fixed bets in your Bet Log staying marked 'open' long after their games had finished. Settlement — grading each pending bet win/loss/push against the final score (or, for pitcher-strikeout props, the starter's actual strikeout total) — only ran once a day, in the early-morning update. Because a full slate plays out over the afternoon and evening, a game that finished at night wasn't graded until the next morning, so bets could show 'open' for up to a day. Settlement now also runs on an evening/overnight cadence, so a bet grades within a couple of hours of its game ending — the same night, not the next day. This is a factual result recap, not betting advice.

Fixed a bet that was automatically voided (because its game was postponed or cancelled) still lingering internally as if unsettled. The bet showed correctly as 'void' on your page, but a bookkeeping marker wasn't cleared, so it was needlessly re-checked on every settlement pass. Voiding a bet now fully closes it out. No change to how a void looks or counts in your record.

Fixed the featured pick's 'Yesterday' recap showing 'Won' (or 'Lost') without its color — a settled result was rendering with the gray 'pending' clock icon instead of the green check for a win or red mark for a loss. The recap's win/loss/pending state was being computed correctly behind the scenes but dropped before it reached the page, so the badge fell back to the neutral pending style. Settled recaps now show green for a win and red for a loss as intended. This is a factual result recap, not betting advice.

Fixed the featured pick's 'Yesterday' recap sometimes staying stuck on 'Pending' after that game had finished. The recap settles to Won or Lost only once the previous game's final result has been ingested, and a late-finishing game (often a West-coast start) frequently isn't available yet when the morning update runs — so the badge could read 'Pending' all day even though the game was long over. The home page now re-checks a still-'Pending' recap when you load it and updates it to Won or Lost the moment the result is in, so it no longer lingers. This is a factual result recap, not betting advice.

Fixed the Dashboard occasionally showing the NEXT day's games as 'today's' picks. Because the next slate's odds and schedule are posted well in advance, and the page was deciding which day is 'today' from your device's own clock and time zone, a browser running ahead of U.S. baseball time could pull in tomorrow's games a day early. The app no longer trusts the browser's local date for the live slate — the current baseball day is now decided on the server (U.S. Pacific baseball calendar), and the picks endpoints refuse to serve a future day, so 'today's' picks are always the current day's slate no matter your device's clock or where you are. Viewing past dates from the calendar is unchanged.

Fixed a browser tab left open for a long time silently breaking. Your signed-in session's access token expires after a while, and previously the app read it once when the tab loaded and never refreshed it — so if you came back to a tab you'd left open, sections like Performance or your Bet Log could load empty or error even though you were still logged in. The app now renews your session automatically: ahead of expiry, whenever you return to the tab, and — as a safety net — the moment any request comes back unauthorized, it silently refreshes and retries that request so the section fills in instead of breaking. You're only sent to the login screen if your session has genuinely expired and can't be renewed. No change to how you log in or out.

Fixed the 'Model Skill' panel on the Performance page showing 'No model data available.' Its per-market summary (picks, calibration, closing-line value, and how often the model's favored side won, moneyline and total runs shown separately) is computed once a day and saved so the page loads fast. The summary now comes straight from the settled-results table it belongs to, and the optional 'exclude degraded predictions' filter is applied as a separate best-effort step — so that filter can no longer come up empty and blank out the whole panel. The page also refuses to save an empty result and recomputes instead, and the affected saved copies have been cleared, so a bad computation can't get stuck. These are factual model outputs, not betting advice, with no profitability claim.

We made the performance numbers we show consistent everywhere. Win rate, record, and ROI now mean exactly the same thing on the Performance page, the Bet Log, and the 'who called it' Results section: a win rate always excludes pushes, records are counted one call per market (moneyline and total runs never combined into a doubled-looking number), and ROI is your realized result net of the sportsbook's cut — a factual record, not a market-advantage claim. Rates based on only a handful of settled bets now carry a plain 'small sample' caveat so an early streak isn't mistaken for a track record, and the number of bets behind a rate is shown alongside it. We also documented how well-calibrated the model's probabilities have actually been, market by market (how often a stated 60% really wins ~60% of the time). These are factual model outputs, not betting advice, with no profitability claim.

The 'Results — who called it' section on the Expected Value Tracker and Dashboard is now collapsible, and its summary tally is clearer. The header stays visible at a glance while the per-game breakdown is tucked away by default to keep the page compact — click it to expand or hide the individual game cards. The call tally is now broken out by market (moneyline and total runs shown separately, each over the number of completed games) instead of combined into a single doubled-looking count. These remain factual model outputs, not betting advice.

A Parlay Calculator is here, under Betting → Parlay Calculator. Build any parlay from the day's slate — moneyline, total runs, and pitcher-strikeout legs — and it shows you the truth about it: our model's estimate of the parlay's true combined probability next to the probability the sportsbook's price implies, plus the expected value per dollar and a plain-language verdict. Pick the sportsbook you're betting with and each leg fills in that book's latest line and odds automatically — including the exact total-runs and pitcher-strikeout lines that book is posting — and every leg shows the model's probability side by side with that book's no-vig probability so you can compare the two. Legs in different games are combined independently; legs in the same game are correlation-adjusted rather than naively multiplied (with a deliberately conservative prior, since a measured same-game correlation isn't available yet), so a same-game parlay's chances are never overstated in your favor. Because sportsbooks price a same-game parlay with their own correlation model, enter the book's posted parlay odds for those and the calculator uses that price. This is a transparency and decision-support tool, not betting advice and not a bet recommendation, with no profitability claim — most parlays are negative expected value once the book's vig is priced in, and the calculator is built to show you that.

Fixed batting lineups sometimes not showing on a game's pick-details page. For a batch of completed games the lineup card was blank even though the lineups were known — a stale cached copy of the page had been saved before that day's lineups posted and was never refreshed. Game pages now only lock in a permanent copy once the lineups are attached, so a page saved too early self-corrects on the next update, and the affected past games have been refreshed. Lineups are factual roster information, not betting advice.

You can now log a strikeout prop into your Bet Log two ways. On a pitcher's Props projection detail, a 'Log this prop' button copies the strikeout line you're viewing — side, book, line, and posted odds — into your log, where you set your stake and save. And to back-log a prop you already placed, the Bet Log now has a 'Log a prop' button: pick a game date within the last 14 days, choose that day's starting pitcher, and enter your side, line, book, odds, and stake — no projection needed. Either way it settles automatically against the pitcher's actual strikeouts once the game is final (Over / Under / Push vs your logged line) and appears in your Bet History like any other bet. This is a bookkeeping convenience, not betting advice and no profitability claim — the logged line, stake, and odds are your own self-reported record; when you log from a projection we store that projection at log time alongside it purely for your reference.

Bet alerts are here. In Settings → Notifications you can now opt in to be told when the model posts qualified plays for the day's slate — by email or browser push (SMS/text is coming soon). Most days nothing fires; you're only notified when there are qualified plays. These are model outputs, not betting advice.

Completed games now show a 'who called it' scorecard. Open a past game's pick-detail page and, alongside the final score, you'll see which side the model favored on the moneyline and total runs and whether that call was correct or missed — and, for the moneyline, whether the closing favorite won too. Pick a past date on the Dashboard or the tracker and a Results section summarizes the same, one card per completed game. It's a factual record shown as plainly for a miss as for a hit — model outputs, not betting advice, with no profitability claim.

Picks that were reconstructed after the fact — re-scored for a past date from the pregame data as it stood that morning, never a live call — now carry a clear 'Backfilled' label on the pick's detail page. These use only point-in-time information (no game outcomes leak in) and are marked so they are never mistaken for a real-time pick.

Dashboard no longer shows the previous day's games before a new day's predictions are published. The 'today' picks fallback was returning the last-cached slate regardless of the requested date; it now only serves picks that match the requested date, and shows an empty state until the day's predictions are ready.

New Props page (under the Betting dropdown in the nav) shows every probable starter's projection for a day at a glance — one card per pitcher with our projected strikeout total, the pitcher's team and matchup, first-pitch time, their last 3 starts' strikeout counts, the 80% range, the sportsbook's posted line, and the model-minus-book gap, sorted so the highest projections lead. Pick any date with the date selector (shared with your Dashboard and EV Tracker), and choose the prop type up top (Strikeouts for now — more coming). Click a card for the full distribution and per-book breakdown. Projections and a transparency comparison only — not betting advice, and we make no profitability claim. To keep the nav uncluttered, Dashboard and EV Tracker now live under that same 'Betting' dropdown (like Research and Admin).

Starting pitcher pages now show a Strikeout Projection — our model's projected strikeout total for that pitcher's next start, shown next to the sportsbooks' posted strikeout line. You get our projected number, a range strip (where the middle 50% of outcomes land, with the median and the book's line marked), and a per-book table comparing the book's de-vigged Over% (its price with the margin removed, so books are comparable) against our model's Over% at the same line, plus the model-minus-book gap. This is a projection and a transparency comparison only — it is not betting advice and we make no profitability claim; single-game strikeout totals are high-variance, so treat it as context, not a play. The projection appears only on days a pitcher is a probable starter and once lines are posted.

The Performance page now shows a Bankroll by Sportsbook breakdown — one row per book with its current balance, net deposits, betting P&L, and growth %. It appears once you've set up at least one book and recorded a deposit (Settings → Sportsbooks), and pulls straight from your tracked bankroll. Growth is return on deposited bankroll with cash flows netted out — kept distinct from ROI (return on stake). Settings → Sportsbooks also gains an opt-in 'Reset baseline' per book: a confirm-gated action that re-bases that book's cost basis to its current balance so growth restarts at 0% from a fresh start — your deposit/withdrawal history is preserved, not deleted. Self-reported bookkeeping; no edge or model claim.

Players are now clickable across pick and team pages, and starting pitchers now show recent form. On a pick's detail page, every batter in the Batting Lineups section and each Probable/Starting Pitcher name now links straight to that player's page (opens in a new tab) — and under each starter you'll see their Last 3 Starts (date, opponent, IP, H, R, K, BB, HR) for quick matchup context. On a team page, the next game's starting pitcher is clickable too. This is navigation and matchup context only — no edge or betting claim.

Each pick's detail page now shows a Line Movement Over Time chart in the Market Action section — across all seven books (Pinnacle, BetMGM, Caesars, FanDuel, DraftKings, Fanatics, Bovada). Pick a book and see how its Moneyline (de-vigged home win probability — vig removed so books are comparable) and Total drifted snapshot-by-snapshot from open to current, with an open→current summary, the net move, and a hover/tap tooltip on each point. For totals you get two views: the line itself (runs) and a de-vigged Over% — because totals lines are sticky at half-run steps and the real market move is often in the juice, which the Over% captures even when the line holds. The book selection stays in sync with the Book Comparison panel; books or markets with no recorded movement show a clean empty state. This is a 'show-your-work' market-context view, not an edge claim: our models have no demonstrated ability to beat the close (best_alpha=0), so read the line drift as context, not a signal.

Zone heatmaps now populate across the full slate. The batter hot-zone × pitcher tendency overlay (the red/blue cell grid on pick and player detail pages) previously only rendered when an overlay happened to be pre-generated. A daily background process now builds overlays for every confirmed batter-vs-starter matchup each morning, so the heatmap shows up consistently — not just for hand-picked showcase pairs. Honest framing: this is a transparency and explainability view of the matchup, not a bet signal.

EV Tracker game times were showing +5 hours too late (e.g. 6:15 PM CDT instead of 1:15 PM CDT). The time formatter was appending a trailing 'Z' to UTC timestamps that already carried an explicit '+00:00' timezone offset, producing an invalid datetime string that browsers treated as local time. Updated the formatter to detect and preserve any existing timezone indicator before parsing — matching the fix already in place on game-detail pages.

Bets on some games were staying 'pending' in the Bet Log instead of settling after the game ended. The MLB Stats API marks a game's status as 'Final (Official)' (status code 'O') rather than plain 'Final' ('F') when the official scorer has reviewed the result — late games in particular were staying in this 'O' state when the nightly settle job ran. The settlement filter now accepts both states, so these bets will settle on the next daily run.

Settings now has a Sportsbooks section for multi-book bankroll bookkeeping. Add each sportsbook you use, set its current balance, and record deposits and withdrawals — so your bankroll growth % reflects only betting results, not cash movement. A deposit is not growth; a withdrawal is not a loss — both are netted out of the baseline. The Performance page now shows an overall Bankroll Growth tile (hidden until you've set up at least one book and recorded a deposit). Growth % is labeled distinctly from ROI: ROI is return on stake/turnover; growth is return on your deposited funds. Self-reported and manual — this is a bookkeeping ledger, not auto-settlement.

The Bet Log now paginates at 25 bets per page, sorted newest-first, with a page counter and Prev / Next controls. The P&L, ROI, and Win Rate summary tiles always reflect your full history for the selected season — not just the visible page.

Matchup heatmaps are now live on pick and player pages. For a batter × pitcher matchup you'll see a strike-zone heatmap of where the batter does damage, overlaid with bubbles showing where the pitcher actually locates each pitch type — with FB / Breaking / Offspeed toggles and a hero 'All' view, per-cell hover details, and a clean empty state for cold-start players without enough data yet. This is an explanatory 'show-your-work' matchup view, not a bet signal: we tested the zone-overlap as a predictive feature and it showed no edge, so the heatmap is for understanding a matchup, not for picking sides.

Line Shopping is now on the EV Tracker. A new 'Line Shopping' section shows model-positive plays ranked by edge, with the best available US price highlighted per play — including which book offers it, the American odds, the model's breakeven price (E9.1), and Pinnacle's fair-value anchor. On each pick's Book Comparison, the best-priced US book for the active pick side is now marked with a 'BEST' badge. This is a line-shopping transparency tool — if you're going to bet this side, here's the best number and where to find it. Our models have no demonstrated market edge (best_alpha=0); the Pinnacle anchor is more truthful than implying our breakeven is the market's.

The CLV confidence bar on each pick's detail page now shows a hover/tap tooltip labeling every visual element: the purple line is the model's P(CLV positive) estimate, the shaded band is its 80% confidence interval, and the gray center line marks 50% (no-signal baseline). The tooltip also shows a plain-English explanation of what the bar means — and for the low-information totals bar, explicitly says the model has no demonstrated signal.

On the game detail page, the win-probability bar now has a book selector. Row of compact pills above the bar lets you switch the orange market reference line between Pinnacle, BetMGM, Caesars, FanDuel, DraftKings, Fanatics, and Bovada — wherever a line is available. The selection stays in sync with the Book Comparison panel. The tooltip and legend update to name whichever book is active. Dashboard and homepage show a consensus market reference (the gray tick is labeled Market).

The win-probability bar on every pick now shows a hover/tap legend that labels each marker: the white line is the model's point estimate, the orange marker is the market implied probability (Pinnacle on the game detail page; consensus on the dashboard), the green band is the 80% credible range, and the gray center line is even odds (50% coin-flip). The tooltip also surfaces concrete numbers attributed to the favored team — e.g. '54% (51–57%) — STL · slight lean' — using the asymmetric CI bounds rather than a symmetric ±. On the game detail page, the CI header now reads 'Win-prob lean' and shows the full attributed range inline; the bar itself is tappable/keyboard-focusable. Accessibility: the bar has a tab stop and aria-label. Single MLB games are high-variance; the calibrated model output spans roughly 43–57% — treat every pick as a lean, not a lock.

Fanatics is now included in the Book Comparison on each pick's detail page. Where Fanatics offers a line, you'll see its moneyline and total prices alongside its de-vigged market probability, model EV, edge, and breakeven price — the same full treatment every other US book receives. Fanatics is also counted in the cross-book '+EV' pill ('N of M books +EV').

Caesars was not appearing in the Book Comparison despite having live lines. The data pipeline was ingesting Caesars under a legacy key ('williamhill_us') that the serving store's book filter didn't recognize. The filter has been updated and Caesars will show correctly after the next odds refresh.

Book Comparison now shows a model breakeven price for each pick — the price at which the model's edge reaches exactly zero. A green chip means the current book price is still better than breakeven; red means the line has moved past the point where the model rates it +EV. Pinnacle's sharp no-vig fair value is always shown alongside for context. This is a transparency tool: our models have no demonstrated market edge, so 'breakeven' is model-relative, not a guarantee.

The Performance page's Win % and CLV stats now measure the side the model actually favored. Previously they reported the raw home-team win rate (Moneyline) and Over rate (Totals) regardless of which side the model picked, so 'Win %' was a base rate rather than the model's accuracy. Win % is now the share of the model's directional picks that won, and Closing Line Value is measured in the pick's direction. Tooltips were rewritten to match. Brier Score (calibration) is unchanged.

The 'Yesterday' badge on the front page now shows the real result of the featured pick. Previously, the badge always appeared green even after a loss — the system was surfacing whichever of yesterday's picks happened to win, not the actual pick that was shown. The pick selection now uses the same logic as today's featured pick, and the badge correctly shows green for a win, red for a loss, and gray for a game that hasn't been settled yet.

The models behind the picks have been upgraded to leak-free versions, and the 'why this pick' explanations now reflect them. The previous models' driver explanations were dominated by a bullpen metric that was partly computed from the game being predicted — an internal data artifact, not a real signal — so nearly every game over-credited the bullpen. The new models remove that leak and are far leaner; the displayed drivers (team strength/ELO, run-based win expectation, and pitching/offense form) now show what the model actually weighs. Picks and probabilities may shift as a result. As always, treat each pick as a lean, not a lock.

The Book Comparison on each pick's detail page was showing odds captured after the game started, which can't be bet. Lines now freeze at the last pre-game snapshot, so every price displayed is one that was actually available before first pitch.

Book Comparison now shows each bookmaker's hold (overround/vig) — the book's built-in margin computed as the sum of both sides' implied probabilities minus 1. A new 'Hold (vig) by book' section lists every available book with its hold percentage for both moneyline and totals markets, with the tightest (lowest-hold) book marked with a ★. The book with the lowest hold also gets a 'LOW VIG' badge in the book selector. Lower hold means less margin built into the price — a tighter, more competitive book to shop. Pinnacle typically runs ~2% hold; US books typically run 4–8%. This is a market-structure fact, not a bet recommendation.
